messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert has been an insurance agent for forty-five years, a life built on the quiet assessment of risk. At seventy-one, he is methodical, precise, and keeps his clients at a professional, unbreachable distance. He has lived alone for decades, a solitude he once saw as a strength but now feels as a crushing weight. For most of his life, he believed he had successfully contained the past, walling it off behind a dam of relentless work and routine. But in the quiet of his impending retirement, the dam has begun to crack, and he has sought help for the flood he can no longer hold back.

The memories that haunt him are not of a single event, but of a season of terror in his childhood. He was seven when his parents left him with his uncle for a summer. The man was a trusted figure, but behind closed doors, fueled by whiskey, he was a monster. Robert remembers the sour, sweet smell of alcohol on his breath, a scent that became synonymous with pain and fear. The fragments of memory that surface now, sixty years later, are intensely vivid, more real than his recollection of yesterday’s breakfast. He feels the rough texture of the living room carpet on his cheek, sees the dust motes dancing in the sliver of light under the door. He remembers one night, after a particularly brutal episode, seeing the flash of red and blue lights through the window and hearing the wail of sirens growing closer, a sound that promised rescue but faded into the distance, leaving him alone in the silence.

Over the decades, Robert developed a host of silent strategies to manage the intrusions. He learned to keep his mind perpetually occupied, filling every spare moment with puzzles, talk radio, or the endless minutiae of insurance policies. When a sudden piece of the past would break through—the image of his uncle’s face, the phantom scent of whiskey—he would immediately begin a mental ritual, reciting the names of state capitals in alphabetical order until the memory receded. This constant mental effort was his way of preventing the worst from happening again, a desperate attempt to control a past that felt dangerously present. He meticulously avoided television shows or films depicting any form of domestic violence, changing the channel at the first sign of a family argument.

The core of Robert’s suffering is a profound sense of betrayal that has metastasized over time, poisoning his perception of the world. He believes the man responsible faced no consequences, a burning injustice that leaves him feeling utterly alone. This conviction that he was failed by those meant to protect him fuels a pervasive sense of threat. He sees danger in the most ordinary situations, believing his body is an enemy that keeps reacting as if he is still that helpless seven-year-old boy. The constant feeling of being unsafe only confirms his belief that he is permanently damaged, that his body’s alarms are broken beyond repair. This appraisal, in turn, makes him hypervigilant to the very things that trigger him; because he believes the world is unsafe, he is always scanning for the approach of a stranger or the distant sound of a siren.

This cycle dominates his daily life. A conversation with a new client at his office, a necessary part of his job, feels like a threat interrogation. The simple act of talking to a stranger can send a jolt of fear through him, instantly activating the deep-seated belief that he was betrayed and is fundamentally unsafe. At home, the feeling of being in danger is a constant companion. He listens intently for any sound that might signal an intruder, his body tensing at the creak of a floorboard or the rustle of leaves outside his window. This state of high alert often triggers the memories he works so hard to suppress; the feeling of being hunted in his own home can suddenly conjure a vivid fragment of the past, making the threat feel immediate and real. To manage this terror, he retreats into his rituals, checking the locks three times, keeping his mind busy until exhaustion finally claims him.

The very strategies he uses to survive have become a cage. The constant mental distraction and avoidance have reinforced his belief that he is too fragile to cope with his own mind, that his body is an enemy he must perpetually outwit. This has kept him isolated, unable to form close relationships for fear of another betrayal. Now, on the cusp of retirement, the prospect of endless, unstructured days terrifies him. The work that served as his primary distraction is ending, and he is afraid of what will rush in to fill the void. He came to therapy not because he believes he can be cured, but because he is exhausted by the vigilance. His only hope, he said quietly in his first session, is to feel safe in his own house before he dies.
